summary: Describes using Elliptic Curve certificates, Elliptic Curve signature schemes, and Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman key agreement within PKINIT, the Kerberos 5 extension that allows public key cryptography for initial authentication. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Kerberos lets you log in once and get tickets. This lets the login use small, strong keys from elliptic curve math, which are more compact than the older kind.

subtitle: Using elliptic curves for Kerberos public-key login

tldr.problem: Kerberos clients and servers need a way to use elliptic curve cryptography (ECC) in PKINIT, the Kerberos extension for public key authentication, rather than just RSA.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies how to use ECC certificates, ECC signatures with multiple hash algorithms, and Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) key agreement within PKINIT, with recommended curves and domain parameters.
tldr.outcome: Systems can use smaller, faster ECC keys instead of RSA, providing equivalent security with shorter key sizes while improving interoperability and performance.

facts.label: Recommended curves
facts.value: P-256 and P-384 (required), plus 13 others from NIST

facts.label: Signature algorithms
facts.value: ECDSA with SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-512

facts.label: Curve types
facts.value: Named curves or custom curves with domain parameters

today: RFC 5349 is an Internet Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It remains the specification for using ECC in Kerberos PKINIT and is in widespread use in modern Kerberos implementations.

sections.title: Why Elliptic Curve Cryptography for Kerberos
sections.content:
Kerberos uses public-key cryptography to authenticate clients and Key Distribution Centers (KDCs). Traditionally, RSA was used, but Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) offers equivalent security with much smaller key sizes. A 256-bit ECC key provides security equivalent to a 3,072-bit RSA key.

This RFC specifies exactly how to use ECC within PKINIT, the Kerberos mechanism for public-key authentication. It covers ECC certificates, digital signatures using ECC, and ECDH for key agreement—the core operations needed for a Kerberos authentication using elliptic curves.
sections.plainLanguage: ECC keys are like using a shorter, smarter code that is just as unbreakable as a longer, plainer code. Kerberos can now use these shorter codes to prove who you are when you log in.

sections.title: ECC Certificates and Signatures
sections.content:
X.509 certificates holding ECC public keys must follow RFC 3279, which defines how ECC algorithms work in certificates. When the client or KDC signs data, they can use one of four ECC signature algorithms paired with matching hash functions:

  • ecdsa-with-Sha1 with id-sha1
  • ecdsa-with-Sha256 with id-sha256
  • ecdsa-with-Sha384 with id-sha384
  • ecdsa-with-Sha512 with id-sha512

Implementations must support SHA-256 signatures and should support SHA-1 for compatibility. The ECC signature schemes are embedded in CMS (Cryptographic Message Syntax) structures used by PKINIT.
sections.plainLanguage: When you sign something with ECC, you pick an ECC key and a hash size. Bigger hash sizes mean slower but safer signatures.

sections.title: Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Key Agreement
sections.content:
During PKINIT authentication, the client and KDC use ECDH to agree on a shared secret key without sending it over the network. The client includes its ECDH public key and the domain parameters (which define the specific elliptic curve being used) in its authentication request. The domain parameters are encoded as part of the public-key algorithm identifier, following RFC 3279.

If the KDC does not accept the requested curve, it sends an error listing acceptable curves in decreasing preference order. The client then chooses one and retries. Once the KDC accepts the curve, it sends back its own ECDH public key. Both sides then compute the shared secret using the x-coordinate of the resulting elliptic curve point, which becomes the material for deriving the session key.
sections.plainLanguage: The client and KDC each pick a secret number and a point on an elliptic curve. They exchange their public points, and both compute the same shared secret without ever sending it directly.

sections.title: Choosing Curves and Key Sizes
sections.content:
The RFC recommends 15 named curves that have Object Identifiers and are standardized by NIST and the Standards for Efficient Cryptography Group. These range from P-192 (192 bits) to P-521 (521 bits), and include both prime-field curves (like P-256, also known as secp256r1) and binary-field curves (like sect163r2).

A key size table in the RFC maps cryptographic strength to appropriate ECC and RSA key sizes. For example, to protect a 128-bit symmetric key, RFC 3766 recommends a 256-bit ECC key (P-256), which is equivalent in strength to a 3,072-bit RSA key. Domain parameters can be either these named curves or custom curves defined locally.

Implementations must support P-256 and P-384 curves for interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: Different curves are like different rules for the secret point math. Some are faster, some are more conservative, but they all come in different sizes. You pick a curve that is big enough to be safe.

sections.title: Security When Using ECDH
sections.content:
The RFC warns of several dangers. First, when receiving an ECDH public key, you must check that it is a valid point on the agreed curve; otherwise, an attacker can leak information about the recipient's private key. This is especially critical if the same private key is reused across multiple authentications.

Second, Kerberos error messages (including the list of acceptable curves) are not integrity protected. An attacker can intercept and modify them to steer clients toward weaker curves. Systems should use local policy to restrict which curves are acceptable.

Third, the choice of curve structure matters. Random curves are more conservative than special curves like Koblitz curves, and curves over prime fields are more conservative than binary fields—but specialized curves can offer efficiency gains. The RFC notes that no concrete attacks are known against most standard curves.
sections.plainLanguage: You need to check that the curve point is real, not fake. Bad actors could trick you into using a weaker curve if they change error messages. Different curves have different pros and cons.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content: RFC 5349 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It provides the specification for using ECC in PKINIT and is widely implemented in modern Kerberos deployments.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is still the official guide for ECC in Kerberos.
